{{Short description|Polytope}}
[[File:Permutoassociahedron.svg|class=skin-invert-image|The permutoassociahedron of dimension <math>2</math> and the correspondence between its vertices and the bracketed permutations of three terms <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, and <math>c</math>.|thumb]]
[[File:Permutoassociahedron3d.svg|class=skin-invert-image|The four facets of the permutoassociahedron of dimension <math>3</math> that share vertex <math>(ab)(cd)</math>. Three of these facets are quadrilaterals and the fourth is a pentagon.|thumb]]
In mathematics, the '''permutoassociahedron''' is an <math>n</math>-dimensional [[polytope]] whose vertices correspond to the bracketings of the [[permutation]]s of <math>n+1</math> terms and whose edges connect two bracketings that can be obtained from one another either by moving a pair of brackets using [[associativity]] or by [[Transposition (mathematics)|transposing]] two consecutive terms that are not separated by a bracket.

The permutoassociahedron was first defined as a [[CW complex]] by [[Mikhail Kapranov]] who noted that this structure appears implicitly in [[Saunders Mac Lane|Mac Lane]]'s [[Coherency (homotopy theory)|coherence]] theorem for symmetric and braided [[Category (mathematics)|categories]] as well as in [[Vladimir Drinfeld]]'s work on the [[Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov equations]].<ref>{{cite journal
| first1=Mikhail M. | last1=Kapranov | authorlink1=Mikhail Kapranov
| title=The permutoassociahedron, Mac Lane's coherence theorem and asymptotic zones for the KZ equation
| journal=Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra
| volume=85
| issue=2
| date=1993
| pages=119–142
| doi=10.1016/0022-4049(93)90049-Y | doi-access=}}</ref> It was constructed as a convex polytope by Victor Reiner and [[Günter M. Ziegler]].<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Reiner | first1=Victor
| last2=Ziegler | first2=Günter M. | authorlink2=Günter M. Ziegler
| title=Coxeter-associahedra
| journal=[[Mathematika]]
| volume=41
| issue=2
| date=1994
| pages=364–393
| doi=10.1112/S0025579300007452}}</ref>

== Examples ==

When <math>n = 2</math>, the vertices of the permutoassociahedron can be represented by bracketing all the permutations of three terms <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, and <math>c</math>. There are six such permutations, <math>abc</math>, <math>acb</math>, <math>bac</math>, <math>bca</math>, <math>cab</math>, and <math>cba</math>, and each of them admits two bracketings (obtained from one another by associativity). For instance, <math>abc</math> can be bracketed as <math>(ab)c</math> or as <math>a(bc)</math>. Hence, the <math>2</math>-dimensional permutoassociahedron is the [[dodecagon]] with vertices <math>a(bc)</math>, <math>a(cb)</math>, <math>(ac)b</math>, <math>(ca)b</math>, <math>c(ab)</math>, <math>c(ba)</math>, <math>(cb)a</math>, <math>(bc)a</math>, <math>b(ca)</math>, <math>b(ac)</math>, <math>(ba)c</math>, and <math>(ab)c</math>.

When <math>n = 3</math>, the vertex <math>((ab)c)d</math> is adjacent to exactly three other vertices of the permutoassociahedron: <math>(ab)(cd)</math>, <math>(a(bc))d</math>, and <math>((ba)c)d</math>. The first two vertices are reached from <math>((ab)c)d</math> via associativity and the third via a transposition. The vertex <math>(ab)(cd)</math> is adjacent to four vertices. Two of them, <math>((ab)c)d</math> and <math>a(b(cd))</math>, are reached via associativity, and the other two, <math>(ba)(cd)</math> and <math>(ab)(dc)</math>, via a transposition. This illustrates that, in dimension <math>3</math> and above, the permutoassociahedron is not a [[simple polytope]].<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Baralić | first1=Djordje
| last2=Ivanović | first2=Jelena
| last3=Petrić | first3=Zoran
| title=A simple permutoassociahedron
| journal=[[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]]
| volume=342
| issue=12
| date=December 2019
| pages=111591
| doi=10.1016/j.disc.2019.07.007
| arxiv=1708.02482}}</ref>

== Properties ==

The <math>n</math>-dimensional permutoassociahedron has
: <math>
n!{2n\choose n}
</math>
vertices. This is the product between the number of permutations of <math>n+1</math> terms and the number of all possible bracketings of any such permutation. The former number is equal to the [[factorial]] <math>(n+1)!</math> and the latter is the <math>n</math>th [[Catalan number]].

By its description in terms of bracketed permutations, the [[N-skeleton|1-skeleton]] of the permutoassociahedron is a [[flip graph]] with two different kinds of flips (associativity and transpositions).
